TANZANITE CON

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We expose a syndicate behind the decade old Tanzanite Con

Summary:
It’s not a new con – but no one has ever been able to ID the clever criminals behind the scam – we have CCTV footage and a PI on their trail.

Diamonds may be a girl’s best friend, but for a group of clever cons, tanzanite is the gem dreams are made of.

Legal to trade in South Africa, these con-artists trick businessmen out of hundreds of thousands of Rands – making off with the cash leaving the victim with a handful of worthless fake stones.


Further information:
The con has been running for at least 10 years. I have a list of 56 case studies dating back to 2011. They all learnt the same the lessons – there’s not quick way to make moolah!

CASE STUDY ONE
Indian businessman from Richardsbay – parted with R700 000 in exchange for tanzanite he believed valued at R1.2 million.

CASE STUDY TWO
Woman in Durban paid over R80 000 – thinking she was holding on to tanzanite worth R130 000.

HOW TO DO IT
We steal a page out of the BBC series The Real Hustle and we re-eanct the con step by step with actors in a James Bond / spy style using silhouettes and clever cuts.

1. The mark (victim) is identified – usually in a car park getting out of their luxury car
2. The conman (usually a foreigner) strikes up a conversation, ask the mark what business he’s in – “what a coincidence” the conman has a business opportunity in the industry – they exchange numbers and move on.
3. A few days later the mark gets a call from the conman – he wants to meet – he needs his help with another deal, and there is an opportunity to make some quick cash.
4. They meet – the conman tell him he has an opportunity to buy tanzanite from a supplier – worth a good couple of hundred thousand but he needs a South African do to the deal, because the supplier doesn’t trust foreigners.
5. The conman takes the mark to have the tanzanite valuated – the “jeweler” confirms it’s worth hundred of thousands – usually quite a bit more than the supplier’s asking price.
6. Back to the supplier, he needs the cash. But the conmen doesn’t have the full amount on him – he convinces the mark to pay a deposit to the supplier, while he goes to arrange the balance. They give the mark the tanzanite to hold to in good faith for the cash.
7. The conmen, supplier and the jeweler are never to be seen again and the tanzanite is worthless glass!

WHY ARE PEOPLE BEING CAUGHT?
It’s believable – the mark/ victim meets a seemingly legitimate jeweler (but it’s one of the conmen) who valuates the stones in person. Then the victim is given the gems to hold on to in exchange for some cash – so the victim is feels secure because they are holding something of value – but it’s worth nothing! And they realize it when it’s too late.

CAN THEY BE CAUGHT?
Yes – The PI has been tracing them and connected two cases to the same team of conmen with the same numbers. We are able to place them at addresses in Durban and hope to make arrests by Friday

Press Release:


Tanzanite Con
Diamonds may be a girl’s best friend, but tanzanite is the gem open to lucrative scams. For years clever con-artists have managed to reel unsuspecting businessmen into the thick of a clever gemstone sale. The attraction? Quick and substantial profits. But once victims pay over hundreds of thousands to the syndicate, all they are left with is a handful of worthless stones. Now, with CCTV footage and a PI on the trail, Carte Blanche catches up with conmen.


Script:


TANZANITE STRUCTURE

VO: Diamonds may be a girl’s best friend, but for a group of sophisticated con-artists, tanzanite is the gem dreams are made of.

LINK: The tanzanite scam isn’t new, for at least the past 10 years clever conmen have convinced their unsuspecting victims with hundreds of thousands of rands for what they hope could be expensive jewellery.

VO: In October 2014, Businessman Brylon Kock parted with R80 000 in cash for what he thought would be the deal of a life time.

BRYLON: 300 000 profit in one day, already you’ve got me mesmerised even if Barack Obama phoned me and said no don’t the deal, I’d say Barack don’t be like that you know you’re on top of the world, I need to make this money!

VO: Private Investigator Sean Peirce says the only thing that’s real about the deal that the money is gone for good.

SEAN: Their names change, their cellphone numbers change, each guy has their role in the scam, but the play is the same.

LINK: The scam always involves three people, the initiator, the seller and the jeweller, and while it seems like a fairly simple arrangement, as the scam progresses, it becomes incredibly complex.

VO: FIRST:
• The mark is made by the initiator, when he is approached usually in a car park as he gets out of a luxury car.
• The conman has a business opportunity linked to the mark’s field of expertise – they exchange numbers and move on.
• A few days later, the mark gets a call. A meeting is set up. This is when the real deal is revealed – the conmen have valuable raw tanzanite stones to sell, they need a lcoal partner and the mark becomes the middleman.
• The initiator takes the mark to have the tanzanite evaluated – with a so-called “jeweler” who confirms it’s worth a fortune.
• Next the mark is convinced to lay out the money – take the stones and collect the profit when he sells to the so-called jeweler.
• The supplier, the initiator and the jeweler make off with the cash - leaving the mark with a handful of worthless stones.

SEAN: It’s well rehearsed, once you throw a question at them, they have an answer for it, they make it too real.

VO: It’s so easy to get sucked in – when they present you with facts and figures for a seemingly legitimate deal.

Brylon says he met two men - a Mr. Kathonga and another called Simon about a construction contract .

BRYLON: As we were about to leave, Simon then asked Mr. Kathongo did you bring any stones with you, and Mr. Kathonga then said, oh yes I did,

VO: With an impressive looking stone in hand, Simon asked Brylon to give him a lift to his jeweler contact.

BRYLON: I said, ok, we are going to be doing business together R50 petrol is nothing.
JOHN: At this point you’re not part of the deal, you’re just the taxi.
BRYLON: 100%

VO: Almost a year later, Richardsbay businessman Reshaab Sikar also met a Mr. Kathonga and a Simon – his original deal was for building warehouses through his engineering company.

RESHAAB: it sounded legit because he knew the area, and he knew the premises that he was talking about, he knew what shipment to bring in, he knew where the market was, the value to sell it at, what sort of budget he was working at to build. So it sounded very legit to me.
JOHN: When they started talking about Tanzanite, did you become more or less interested?
RESHAAB: Very much more interested.
JOHN: Why is it?
RESHAAB: It sounded like a walk in walk out deal.// I go in I buy the stuff and I sell it to the lady who is buying – from R700 000 – it was said that evaluated at R1.2 million –
JOHN: That’s massive profits in double quick time.

LINK: These scams aren’t opportunistic, and they are not limited to just the city of Durban alone – they are run by syndicates and splinter groups run similar scams in cities across the country. SYNDICATE LINKS

JAY: We don’t believe it is one or two gangs, it’s just that people have realised that this is an easy way to make money,. INT 3 M1

VO: PI Sean says the biggest challenge in cracking these cases is tracking down the conmen…..

SEAN: it’s not easy these days to follow up a complaint where the names and the cell numbers don’t match // where do you go? You get to a dead end. INT 2 M3

VO: That’s until you a tip off comes in

LINK: We have information that a deal is about to go down, we’re at a fairly busy intersection in Durban – police are positioned in various locations in and around the spot where we believe the transaction is going to happen and any minute now the suspect is due to arrive.

VO: We got the signal from Sean and rushed to the scene – the police had just interrupted the deal. The con-artist had no where to run.

JOHN: Are you part of this Tanzanite scam?
SUSPECT: No…

VO: While he claimed ignorance, construction contractor Nick XX says that’s not true – the meeting was to exchange R20 000 in cash for tanzanite.

JOHN: So you are here this morning to give money to this gentleman here.
MARK: Yes, these two gentlemen here will take me through to meet Mr. Kathonga to pick up the stones.

VO: It’s seems the same Mr Kathonga from Reshaab’s CCTV footage was set make an appearance in this con too.

JOHN: Are you saying that the gentleman that we’ve just spoken to is lying?
SUSPECT: Yes, yes, because for me it was construction.

VO: Seemingly spinning more lies, the police took the suspect away for questioning.

There are at least 60 cases dating back to 2011 on local scam websites.

LINK: So, how do you convince the mark that this fairly impressive looking stone is in fact tanzanite. Well key to the process is a device that the scamsters say is able to determine it’s clarity and crucially it’s value.

VO: Brylon says they had him hook, line and sinker.

BRYLON: They test it with a proper machine, a testing machine, after he weighed the stone, he puts his nice glass on, put it’s up towards the sun and say ooh look at this colour, I love this colour, you know, there after he puts the machine on it and it goes, it goes beep, beep, beep – it’s starts making all these things and you look, you know for sure this guy is a tester, he is looking the part. INT 3 M1

VO: But Qualified Gemologist Chris de Beer says while it’s completely legal to trade Tanzanite it’s impossible to do proper mobile testing – it’s all part of the con. The quickest way to check is with a polarascope to determine crystal optical properties.

CHRIS: You cross the Polaroid filters and you shine a light through it, if it is a birefringent stone, which tanzanite is and you rotate the stone will blink. Where if it is glass, the stone will stay dark.

VO: To sweeten the deal, the conmen promise SARS certification for the stones - the documents never materialise, because the so-called tanzanite is just coloured glass.

RESHAAB: 700 thousand rand and I’ve taken a long time to save that money and just to let it go was very heartbreaking.

LINK: These days it’s not unusual for business deals to be done outside of the boardroom, at coffee shops and on golf courses but what is inescapable is that almost all of those deals contain an element of risk.

JOHN: Ae you be surprised that people are falling for this?
CHRIS: Not really // usually if it has just been mined and it comes out of the earth they wash it, they clean it they get rid of that stuff. // it only gets to the blue colour once it’s been heat treated. //, everything burns off, so you would have a clean crystal line things.

VO: Even when Reshaab wanted to have the stones tested independently the conmen put his concerns to rest – Reshaad was so convinced he was willing to risk his life savings on this new business opportunity.
.
RESHAAB: IT can happen to anybody, anybody – it’s so well rehearsed, there is no stuttering about it, there’s no I’ll get back to you, there’s no lack of information.

SEAN: You can’t beat them at their own game, but you can never be to clever.

VO: But they did slip up… Reshaad’s meeting was captured on CCTV footage.

It appears the conmen had changed roles.

BRYLON: When I looked at the footage. I saw Mr. Kathonga, is no more the businessman, Mr Kathonga is now the seller

But there’s no denying that the modus operandi is still the same. It was the games changer Sean had been waiting. Armed with the footage he too the streets. The footage will be critical in connecting the dots moving forward.

SEAN: Putting the pieces together, the faces, the cell numbers, getting the different people that have been caught to say who is this person on this picture, I have two people that have given me two different names – the challenges are very real because we don’t know who they are, but with the video footage now, we can identify them.

VO: Police Spokesperson Col Naicker says this arrest is just a starting point for investigators.

JAY: They operate under in a veil of secrecy //most cases it’s my word against yours, so we actually need to catch the guy in the act of handing over the gems and receiving the money.

VO: If it sounds too good to be true it usually is.

CHRIS: if it was that valuable it won’t end up in the street. If I had a big chunk like that I wouldn’t know where to take it myself, I wouldn’t know who to sell it to.
BRYLON: you feel so small, that even whatever credentials , what ever diplomas, whatever degrees you have behind you, that means nothing at that point, all that fades away and you start to klap yourself and say but listen, how could you not see it. // but at that time these guys take control of your mind and yah.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We expose a syndicate behind the decade old Tanzanite Con
metadata.Summary: It’s not a new con – but no one has ever been able to ID the clever criminals behind the scam – we have CCTV footage and a PI on their trail. Diamonds may be a girl’s best friend, but for a group of clever cons, tanzanite is the gem dreams are made of. Legal to trade in South Africa, these con-artists trick businessmen out of hundreds of thousands of Rands – making off with the cash leaving the victim with a handful of worthless fake stones.
metadata.Further information: The con has been running for at least 10 years. I have a list of 56 case studies dating back to 2011. They all learnt the same the lessons – there’s not quick way to make moolah! CASE STUDY ONE Indian businessman from Richardsbay – parted with R700 000 in exchange for tanzanite he believed valued at R1.2 million. CASE STUDY TWO Woman in Durban paid over R80 000 – thinking she was holding on to tanzanite worth R130 000. HOW TO DO IT We steal a page out of the BBC series The Real Hustle and we re-eanct the con step by step with actors in a James Bond / spy style using silhouettes and clever cuts. 1. The mark (victim) is identified – usually in a car park getting out of their luxury car 2. The conman (usually a foreigner) strikes up a conversation, ask the mark what business he’s in – “what a coincidence” the conman has a business opportunity in the industry – they exchange numbers and move on. 3. A few days later the mark gets a call from the conman – he wants to meet – he needs his help with another deal, and there is an opportunity to make some quick cash. 4. They meet – the conman tell him he has an opportunity to buy tanzanite from a supplier – worth a good couple of hundred thousand but he needs a South African do to the deal, because the supplier doesn’t trust foreigners. 5. The conman takes the mark to have the tanzanite valuated – the “jeweler” confirms it’s worth hundred of thousands – usually quite a bit more than the supplier’s asking price. 6. Back to the supplier, he needs the cash. But the conmen doesn’t have the full amount on him – he convinces the mark to pay a deposit to the supplier, while he goes to arrange the balance. They give the mark the tanzanite to hold to in good faith for the cash. 7. The conmen, supplier and the jeweler are never to be seen again and the tanzanite is worthless glass! WHY ARE PEOPLE BEING CAUGHT? It’s believable – the mark/ victim meets a seemingly legitimate jeweler (but it’s one of the conmen) who valuates the stones in person. Then the victim is given the gems to hold on to in exchange for some cash – so the victim is feels secure because they are holding something of value – but it’s worth nothing! And they realize it when it’s too late. CAN THEY BE CAUGHT? Yes – The PI has been tracing them and connected two cases to the same team of conmen with the same numbers. We are able to place them at addresses in Durban and hope to make arrests by Friday
